activities.anchor: By symmetry each reaction takes half
activities.caption: one line of the reaction solve is wrong — find it
activities.name: fbReactionSpot

config.prompt: A student solves the off-centre load. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 — the whole of planar statics
A 10 kN point load sits 2 m from the left support of a 6 m simple span
Take moments about the right support: R_left × 6 = 10 × 4
By fairness the load splits evenly: 5 kN and 5 kN
R_left = 6.67 kN and R_right = 3.33 kN — the closer support carries more
config.correction: Moments decide, not fairness: the lever arms are unequal, so the reactions are unequal — R_left × 6 = 10 × 4 gives 6.67 kN, leaving 3.33 kN.
config.why: Moments about the far support is the standard trick that isolates one unknown at a time.

activities.anchor: Design is making every link in that chain exist, continuous, and adequate
activities.caption: trace the load path, slab to soil
activities.name: fbLoadPathOrder

config.prompt: Follow the force — stack the load path in order:
items: The slab — the load enters and it bends, delivering edge loads
The beams — they bend and deliver reactions
The columns — carry it down in compression
The foundation — spreads it onto soil at pressures the soil can bear (100–600 kPa)
config.why: The collapse modes are almost always broken or never-imagined load paths — a column removed from under a transfer beam; a wall that was load-bearing but not accounted for.

activities.anchor: Drag the load and span below and watch the moment parabola respond
activities.caption: pin the L² tax on the multiplier scale
activities.name: fbSpanPlace

config.prompt: The peak moment carries an L² tax. Double a beam's span — by what multiplier does the peak moment grow?
config.why: M_max = wL²/8: doubling L quadruples the peak while doubling w only doubles it — the L² tax that decides so much structural economics.

activities.anchor: That single exponent is why floor joists
activities.caption: true or false — the geometry of stiffness
activities.name: fbDepthJudge

statements.s: Depth enters the second moment of area cubed, width only linearly.
Doubling a beam's depth multiplies I by 8; doubling its width merely by 2.
statements.why: Same width, same area, same material — geometry alone buys the factor.

statements.s: A wider beam is as good as a deeper one — material is material.
statements.why: Material where the stress is — distance from the neutral axis is leverage over bending.

statements.s: Sections are placed on edge because of that one power of depth.
statements.why: The I-beam concentrates its material in distant flanges for exactly this reason.

statements.s: "Just use more of the same section" is usually the smart fix.
statements.why: Rarely — shape beats quantity when the exponent is on your side.

activities.anchor: Each bar then uses its entire cross-section uniformly
activities.caption: the zero-force member decision
activities.name: fbTrussBranch

config.root: You inherit a triangulated skeleton from an earlier design team. A review flag: one member carries no force under the drawn load case.

start.text: The member reads zero force. What is the call?

choices.label: Remove it — dead weight is dead weight
choices.feedback: A rookie's optimisation — it can trigger collapse under a load case nobody drew.

choices.label: Keep it — its role is stability
choices.feedback: Right — geometry often keeps members whose only task is keeping the shape rigid.

choices.label: Thin it down to a token size
choices.feedback: Thinning still removes the brace — the task was never carried by area alone.

why.text: Why does the triangulated frame beat a bending beam per kilogram?

choices.label: Every member works its full area in pure tension or compression
choices.feedback: No bending anywhere — the efficiency the I-beam only approaches.

choices.label: Because triangles look stronger
choices.feedback: The real reason is geometric: a pin-jointed triangle cannot change shape without changing a bar's length.

risk.text: The removed brace lets the panel shear into a parallelogram under the un-drawn load case — collapse. Method of joints or sections would have shown the stability role.

end.text: Rigid by construction, axial by loading — the railway century's bridge vocabulary, solvable by hand.

config.why: The triangle cannot change shape without changing a bar's length — rigidity by construction, the efficiency the I-beam only approaches.

activities.anchor: the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge's 1,991 m main span (1998)
activities.caption: pin the long-span record on the ladder
activities.name: fbRecordPlace

config.prompt: Pin the long-span record holder's main span on the ladder:
config.why: Suspension owns the record because tension members pay no buckling penalty and cable self-weight grows gently with length; cable-stayed dominates the 200–1,000 m range on stiffness and economy.

activities.anchor: The only casualty was a dog left in the stranded last car
activities.caption: bet the mechanism before the modern finding
activities.name: fbFlutterPredict

config.q: A wind the deck's strength could resist easily tore it apart. What was the mechanism?
choices: Resonance with the wind — the classroom myth
Aeroelastic flutter — wind coupling with the deck's torsional mode
config.why: Modern analysis, not the myth: the deck was shallow, stiff in bending, and fatally flexible in twist — the trapezoid box girder you see everywhere is Tacoma's signature, written in cross-section.

activities.anchor: before a beam ever carries load
activities.caption: reinforced vs prestressed — drag the divider
activities.name: fbPrestressCompare

config.prompt: One material, two strategies — drag the divider across the beam:

before.label: reinforced concrete
before.text: Strong in compression, weak in tension: when bending pulls the bottom face, cracks open — and spans die near 20 m.

after.label: prestressed
after.text: Tendons jacked and anchored inside the member squeeze the concrete first; the in-service forces merely relieve that pre-compression — net tension never appears, cracks never open, and spans that died near 20 m run to 40 m and beyond.

config.why: Freeway viaducts, parking structures, floor slabs — the century's infrastructure is largely this trick, working invisibly inside the grey.
